Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for sending your article entitled "Chromatin accessibility dynamics and single cell transcriptomics reveal new regulators of neural progenitor regeneration" for peer review at eLife. Your article is being evaluated by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation is being overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Marianne Bronner as the Senior Editor.

All of the reviewers find the manuscript interesting and think that it will be potentially very useful to the community. That said, they also raise substantial concerns that will require major revisions.

Reviewer #1:

The manuscript by Kakebeen et al., is addressing a fundamental question in developmental and regenerative biology. With the realization of human therapies for nervous system regeneration after spinal cord injury, it is important to understand the strategies for regeneration that nature has already solved. The advent of new techniques such as scRNAseq and ATAC-seq have generated opportunities to study changes in cell state and type in complex cell populations, which Kakebeen et al., has made progress with here. Considering the authors are addressing a classic question in regenerative biology using the latest techniques, they’re of great value to the study. Overall, the ATACseq and scRNAseq seem robust, but there are some significant flaws in the design of the study that limit the interpretation that can be made by the readers. These problems are described below.

1) The choice of pax6:GFP as the driver instead of Sox2 is a major drawback of the paper, unless major reinterpretation of the data is performed. The impression made from the Introduction and Results is that the study focuses on all NPCs. Based upon previous literature, this is likely not the case. Pax6 plays a well-established role in determining the dorsal/ventral fate of NSCs in the developing spinal cord across vertebrates, namely the pMN domain, and is expressed in a restricted intermediate dorsal/ventral zone of the vertebrate spinal cord (Pituello, 1997; Reimer et al., 2009). The image in Figure 1B needs to be of higher quality in order to determine the expression pattern of the transgene, but it looks to be and is most likely expressed in a canonical fashion in the intermediate D/V zone of the spinal cord. I would suggest a thinner cryosection and a zoom in on the spinal cord specifically. Pax6 has also been associated with controlling cell cycle exit in neural progenitor cells towards differentiation (Bel-Vialar, Medevielle, and Pituello, 2007; Osumi et al., 2008), which should be kept in mind throughout the study. Also, canonical D/V pax6 expression is maintained in mature axolotl salamander spinal cords and dorsal/ventral position of NSCs mainly remain stable after spinal cord regeneration in the axolotl (McHedlishvili et al., 2007). Considering all interpretation of the manuscript is under the assumption that all NPCs are marked and differentiation is not specific to a D/V region, the interpretation is missing a lot of likely very interesting findings on pax6 function and D/V patterning during spinal cord regeneration. As is, it is difficult to interpret exactly what the cell population the pax6:GFP cells are labeling and what they are differentiating into during regeneration (see next statement).

2) It should be explained why cre/lox lineage tracing was not used in the study. As presented, it is unclear if the cell population that is being sorted is exclusively the NSCs or does it include the neurons they differentiate into. Based upon the gene families that were identified from ATACseq including genes involved in neuritogenesis and growth cone formation, it is likely the authors also sorted differentiated neurons or cells in the process of differentiating. It is known that GFP protein can last for days long after the transgene is not expressed. Use of a Sox2 Cre driver Xenopus mated with a fluorescent cre reporter would have overcome the ambiguity of the cells that are being studied and provide a clear trajectory of NSC to differentiated cell types.

3) The in situ hybridizations in Figure 5 do not support the sequencing data. At stage 41, both genes look to be expressed in all mesodermal tissue such as muscle. In subsection “Gene regulatory network prediction reveals pbx3 and meis1 as candidate

regulators of neuronal regeneration”, it states "Of these, pbx3 was the most restricted to the neural lineage (Supp. 3 E/G)". This is emphasized again in the Discussion. The in situ hybridization shows pbx3 is expressed throughout the mesenchyme of the regenerating tail at 48dpa. It will be important to perform cross sections of tissues to show expression in the expected domains, which will likely be the intermediate DV regions of the spinal cord (see new interpretations of pax6 cells above). I would suggest commercially available FISH such as hybridization chain reaction (molecularinstruments.com) or RNAscope that has higher resolution in the cellular level.

Reviewer #2:

The manuscript by Kakebeen et al., ("Chromatin accessibility dynamics and single cell transcriptomics reveal new regulators of neural progenitor regeneration") investigates the transcriptional changes in neural tissue accompanying tail regeneration in Xenopus tropicalis tadpoles. The key findings are that (1) the initial transcriptional response promotes neuronal differentiation, followed within 3 days by an increase in expression of genes associated with cell proliferation; and (2) meis1 and pbx3 emerge as important regulators of the neural regenerative response. This first finding in particular is novel and challenges the fundamental assumption that cell dedifferentiation and proliferation are the initial steps in regeneration. The novelty and potential significance of these observations, together with the overall quality of the work, merit publication in eLife. Moreover, the manuscript is very clearly presented, and the logical flow of the computational analyses is easy to follow.

I have two points of concern. The first is that, while the authors claim that pbx3 is predicted to be a key transcriptional regulator of the neural regenerative response, the results in Figure 5 indicate that only a very small proportion of neural cells express pbx3. (I found Figure 5E-5F somewhat confusing, and it may be that clarification of the figure legends will address this issue). If my understanding of these results is correct, however, then I suggest the authors revise the text, since, as written, it implies that pbx3 is critical to the entire regenerative response.

The second is in regard to the morpholino oligonucleotide (MO) experiments. The authors use two different MOs for each of the two targets, in lieu of a mispair control. While the pbx3 MOs lead to quite similar results, the meis1 MOs produce somewhat distinct phenotypes (compare Figure 5 C-D, 5W-X). This may be a sample size issue, or it may arise from the apparent greater effectiveness of MO1 vs MO2. Given the ongoing discussion regarding MO use, I would like to see the authors address this point in some way, either experimentally (e.g., a western blot comparing effectiveness of the two MOs in regulating endogenous pbx3 [Abcam has an antibody that works for mammalian species and zebrafish], but other strategies would be suitable) or via discussion in the text, which might also include results of computational comparisons to identify any other predicted targets.

Reviewer #3:

In this manuscript, Kakebeen et al. analyzed chromatin accessibility and single cell transcriptomes from pax6-driven GFP positive cells during Xenopus tail regeneration. The authors utilized transgenic pax6:GFP to sort neural progenitor cells (NPCs) throughout this study. They used deep sequencing, ATACseq, and SCseq to define transcripts, biological processes, and transcription factors that are central to spinal cord regeneration in the regenerating Xenopus tail. The authors concluded that NPCs place an early priority on neuronal differentiation early after injury, and prioritize proliferation at later stages of regeneration. They go on to perform morpholino-based functional analysis on two candidate transcription factors, and concluded that meis1 and pbx3 are required for spinal cord development and regeneration.

Overall, bulk RNA-seq, ATACseq and SCseq offer a powerful combination of tools to infer new insights into the cellular and temporal regulation of endogenous spinal cord regeneration Xenopus. The battery of analyses performed on these datasets is well-executed, revealing an early emphasis (6 hpa) on neuronal differentiation and a later emphasis on neural progenitor replenishment (72 hpa). The authors also use their scRNA-seq dataset to define new markers for neural cell types. However, this hypothesized temporal regulation of NPC injury responses is weakened by the following concerns:

1) The entire study is based on the assumption that pax6 is a general marker for NPCs prior to and during regeneration, and that pax6:GFP recapitulates endogenous pax6 expression throughout the time course of regeneration. While all the conclusions from this study are based on these assumptions, pax6:GFP transgenic animals were poorly characterized (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

– Higher magnification images and extensive co-labeling with well-established NPC markers throughout regeneration are critical for this study.

– Confirming that the transgene recapitulates endogenous pax6 expression is also critical for the study. The authors state pax6:GFP is consistent with developmental expression of pax6, but this is assuming regeneration will fully recapitulate development, which is not always the case. An additional concern is the stability of GFP over fine time windows as narrow as 6 hours.

– From the low mag images in Figure 1D, it seems that the transgene is not restricted to the spinal cord. This observation is further supported by scRNA-seq (Figure S3A), which indicates that pax6 is expressed in many cell types beyond NPCs.

2) Even with a full characterization of the transgene, this reviewer is always concerned about drawing conclusions based on a single genetic tool. In this case, it is impossible to rule out the presence of pax6 negative progenitor cells that differentially contribute proliferation versus differentiation at different time points after injury. Further, equally impossible is to rule out technical cell dissociation limitations that may cause differential cell representations in the analysis.

3) The main premise of the study is that NPCs place an early priority on neuronal differentiation before prioritizing proliferation. This is an interesting and potentially relevant observation that warrants experimental support.

– Detailed elucidation of cell proliferation (rostral and caudal to the lesion), migration, and differentiation are recommended in this case.

– These studies would also address the possibility that proliferation is occurring rostral to lesion and that NPCs are recruited into the regenerate where they differentiate into neurons.

– The authors supported their conclusion that NPC proliferation is not abundant until 72 hpa by referencing Love et al., 2011 and their own work (Chang et al., 2017). Chang et al., 2017 does not mention cell proliferation and instead shows an emphasis on immune response at 72 hpa in whole tail. Love et al., 2011 does show an increase in cell proliferation in whole tail at 72 hpa. To support the authors' conclusion that this boost in cell proliferation is indeed happening in the spinal cord, a marker for cell proliferation should be used in the pax6:GFP expressing tadpoles following tail transection.

4) The authors followed up on their SCseq findings by performing functional analyses for meis1 and pbx3. Unfortunately, these studies present a number of major concerns that dampen the excitement about the study.

– The morpholino experiments do not follow recent guidelines for morpholino use. Proper controls are recommended in this case.

– It is unclear how the authors concluded CNS/spinal cord developmental defects based on the severe morpholino phenotypes that were obtained even at the lower doses. These phenotypes are consistent with generic, overall toxicity phenotypes that are common to morpholinos.

– The severe developmental phenotypes caused by meis1 and pbx3 cloud the interpretation of regeneration phenotypes in these morphants.

– Neurofilament stains for uninjured wildtype and morphant animals should be included in Figure 6.

– What is the effect of meis1 and pbx3 morpholinos on cell proliferation in both injured and uninjured tadpoles?

– The authors claim meis1 is required for the neuronal differentiation occurring at early timepoints during spinal cord regeneration. They show that axons in the regenerating tail are disorganized in meis1 morphants, but are these neurons the appropriate neuron type?

2) The addition of Sox2 antibody staining and its overlap with pax6:GFP is informative. There is a small number of Sox2+ cells that are pax6:GFP negative, which the authors address in the text. However, reviewer 3 has two concerns with this data:

a) Sox2/pax6:GFP co-labelling is performed during tadpole development. This approach assumes pax6:GFP and Sox2 co-expression behave similarly in regeneration as in development, which is not necessarily the case.

b) The authors do not address pax6:GFP+ Sox2- cells. These cells, which are observed by histology and scRNA-seq analysis, could affect data interpretation in Figures 2 and 3.

3) pax6:GFP- Sox2+ NPCs do exist. How are these cells contributing to the differences seen in cell proliferation and differentiation during different stages of regeneration? Perhaps these are the pH3+ cells present at 24 hpa. These pax6:GFP- Sox2+ cells appear to be fewer in number, but their presence should be more clearly acknowledged in the text.

claims.claim: Xenopus tadpoles are able to undergo scarless healing and full regeneration of the limb, spinal cord, or tail after injury.
claims.source: In contrast to mammals, Xenopus tadpoles are able to undergo scarless healing and full regeneration of the limb, spinal cord, or tail after injury (Beck et al., 2009; Kakebeen and Wills, 2019; Lee-Liu et al., 2017; Tseng and Levin, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claims.claim: The regenerative capacity of Xenopus declines during metamorphosis and is lost in the adult.
claims.source: While lifelong regenerative healing is a characteristic shared by many amphibians and fish, the regenerative capacity of Xenopus declines during metamorphosis, and is lost in the adult (Filoni and Bosco, 1981; Mitogawa et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: Developmental signaling pathways such as Wnt, FGF, BMP, TGF-ß, Notch and Shh are upregulated during regeneration and are required for full regeneration of the limb, tail, and spinal cord.
claims.source: In particular, developmental signaling pathways such as Wnt, FGF, BMP, TGF-ß, Notch and Shh are upregulated, and are required for full regeneration of the limb, tail, and spinal cord (Beck et al., 2003; Ho and Whitman, 2008; Slack et al., 2008; Taniguchi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: Numerous genes associated with embryonic development are re-expressed during regeneration.
claims.source: Genome-wide transcriptomic studies have confirmed that numerous genes associated with embryonic development are re-expressed during regeneration (Chang et al., 2017; Lee-Liu et al., 2014; Love et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: The regenerating axolotl limb shows a transcriptional convergence between all connective tissue cell types, associated with the formation of the undifferentiated limb blastema.
claims.source: The regenerating axolotl limb shows a transcriptional convergence between all connective tissue cell types, associated with the formation of the undifferentiated limb blastema (Gerber et al., 2018)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claims.claim: In the Xenopus tail, cell type identities are kept clearly intact as regeneration progresses.
claims.source: while in the Xenopus tail, cell type identities are kept clearly intact as regeneration progresses (Aztekin et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claims.claim: Pax6 is a highly conserved paired box transcription factor essential for central nervous system development.
claims.source: Pax6 is a highly conserved paired box transcription factor essential for central nervous system development (Bel-Vialar et al., 2007; Osumi et al., 2008; Walther and Gruss, 1991).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: GFP expression in transgenic tadpoles includes much of the same domain as the NSC marker Sox2.
claims.source: GFP expression in transgenic tadpoles included much of the same domain as the NSC marker Sox2 (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D showing colocalization of GFP and Sox2.

claims.claim: Both nuclear Sox2 and cytoplasmic GFP driven by pax6 are localized medially around the central canal, while markers associated with differentiated neurons such as Dcx and neurofilament are largely found in the spinal cord periphery.
claims.source: Notably, both nuclear Sox2 and cytoplasmic GFP driven by pax6 are localized medially around the central canal, while markers associated with differentiated neurons such as Dcx and neurofilament are largely found in the spinal cord periphery (Figure 1E,F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 1E and 1F showing spatial distribution of markers.

claims.claim: pax6:GFP+ cells can be clearly identified in the regenerating tail as early as 6hpa.
claims.source: We found that pax6:GFP+ cells can be clearly identified in the regenerating tail as early as 6hpa (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1G showing GFP+ cells at 6hpa.

claims.claim: By 24hpa, the GFP+ cells are found in the bulb of the neural ampulla.
claims.source: By 24hpa, the GFP+ cells are found in the bulb of the neural ampulla (Beck et al., 2009; Stefanelli, 1951).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: By 72hpa, GFP+ cells are present all along the anteroposterior axis of the regenerated spinal cord.
claims.source: By 72hpa, GFP+ cells are present all along the anteroposterior axis of the regenerated spinal cord.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observations from the regeneration timecourse experiment.

claims.claim: The pax6 libraries cluster away from the clustered all-tissue libraries in multi-dimensional scaling analysis.
claims.source: We found that the pax6 libraries cluster away from the clustered all-tissue libraries (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2B showing MDS plot.

claims.claim: The majority of peaks called were located within 500 bp of a transcription start site for both all tissue and pax6 libraries.
claims.source: The majority of peaks called were located within 500 bp of a transcription start site for both all tissue and pax6 libraries, confirming that the majority of ATAC-Seq signal is concentrated in nucleosome-depleted promoters, as expected (Buenrostro et al., 2013; Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2C and citation to the ATAC-Seq method paper.

claims.claim: Upstream of the pax6 TSS, all pax6 library timepoints share a peak that is absent in all-tissue libraries.
claims.source: By contrast, upstream of the pax6 TSS, all pax6 library timepoints share a peak that is absent in all-tissue libraries (Figure 2D, right).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2D showing IGV browser tracks.

claims.claim: 3604 regions were more accessible in the pax6 libraries than the all-tissue libraries.
claims.source: We identified 3604 regions that were more accessible in the pax6 libraries than the all-tissue libraries, which we assigned to the nearest TSS, and used the associated gene names as input for gene ontology (GO) analysis using gProfileR2 (Raudvere et al., 2019; Figure 2E–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the differential accessibility analysis and reference to Figure 2E-F.

claims.claim: Genes with increased accessibility in pax6:GFP+ cells showed statistically significant enrichment for neural-associated terms such as 'Neurogenesis', 'Nervous system development', and 'Neuron differentiation.'
claims.source: Genes with increased accessibility in pax6:GFP+ cells showed statistically significant enrichment for neural-associated terms such as 'Neurogenesis', 'Nervous system development', and 'Neuron differentiation,' confirming the neural progenitor identity of our pax6:GFP cells (Figure 2F, top, and Supplementary file 1c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: 5251 regions are more accessible in all-tissue libraries than pax6 libraries.
claims.source: The reverse analysis identified 5251 regions that are more accessible in all-tissue libraries than pax6 libraries, which are associated with broad GO categories relating to ubiquitous cellular processes (i.e. 'Cellular biosynthetic process', 'Transcription from RNA Polymerase II', and Cellular metabolic process') (Figure 2F, bottom, Supplementary file 1d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the differential accessibility analysis and reference to Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Genes preferentially accessible at 6hpa called six families of GO terms including 'Nephron Tubule Morphogenesis'.
claims.source: We first examined genes associated with regulatory regions that are uniquely accessible at 6hpa. Genes preferentially accessible at 6hpa called six families of GO terms (Figure 3D). Notably, 'Nephron Tubule Morphogenesis' was well represented
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Regions most accessible at the 24hpa timepoint recovered two main families of GO terms, the largest of which was 'Neuron Development'.
claims.source: We then identified regions that were most accessible at the 24hpa timepoint. This analysis recovered two main families of GO terms, the largest of which was 'Neuron Development' (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The majority of genes that call the 'Neuron Development' GO term become more accessible from 6 to 24hpa, but lose that accessibility at 72hpa.
claims.source: Strikingly, the majority of genes that call this GO term become more accessible from 6 to 24hpa, but lose that accessibility at 72hpa (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3H showing heatmap of accessibility.

claims.claim: Processes prioritized at 72hpa resulted in five main GO families being called including 'neuronal precursor cell proliferation'.
claims.source: Finally, we assessed the processes being prioritized at 72hpa. This analysis resulted in five main GO families being called (Figure 3F), including 'neuronal precursor cell proliferation'.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Cell cycle and proliferation related terms were absent at the 6hpa and 24hpa timepoints.
claims.source: Notably, cell cycle and proliferation related terms were absent at the 6hpa and 24hpa timepoints.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the absence of these terms in GO analysis at earlier timepoints.

claims.claim: The regions calling 'neuronal precursor cell proliferation' were all more accessible at 72hpa than the 24hpa timepoint.
claims.source: The regions calling this term were all more accessible at 72hpa than the 24hpa timepoint, however about half were not differentially accessible with respect to the uninjured tail (Figure 3I)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3I showing heatmap of accessibility.

claims.claim: A total of 781 uninjured cells and 296 cells from 24hpa cells fell into neural clusters.
claims.source: A total of 781 uninjured cells and 296 cells from 24hpa cells fell into neural clusters, which comprised NPC/NSCs (defined by expression of sox2), transitioning neurons (neurog1; neurod1), and differentiated neurons (elavl4) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-Seq analysis and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Eight unique sub-clusters were identified within neural cells, including spinal cord progenitors, floor plate progenitors, differentiating neurons, interneurons, motor neurons, vulnerable motor neurons, motor neurons (leptin+), and dopaminergic neurons.
claims.source: To gain the highest-possible resolution of cell types within these broad neural clusters, we subsetted neural cells, re-performed dimensionality reduction and called eight unique sub-clusters, including spinal cord progenitors, floor plate progenitors, differentiating neurons, interneurons, motor neurons, vulnerable motor neurons, motor neurons (leptin+), and dopaminergic neurons (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-Seq analysis and reference to Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Unlike the connective tissues in the axolotl limb, which lose cell heterogeneity of gene expression after injury, neural cells in the 24hpa Xenopus spinal cord maintain heterogeneous gene expression.
claims.source: Unlike the connective tissues in the axolotl limb, which lose cell heterogeneity of gene expression after injury (Gerber et al., 2018), neural cells in the 24hpa Xenopus spinal cord maintain heterogeneous gene expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published research on axolotl limb regeneration.

claims.claim: At 24hpa, there is a decrease in the percent of NPCs and differentiating neurons with respect to the uninjured cells.
claims.source: Indeed, at 24hpa, we observe a decrease in the percent of NPCs and differentiating neurons with respect to the uninjured cells (Figure 4D–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 4D-G showing sunburst diagrams.

claims.claim: At 24hpa, there is an expansion in differentiated neuronal clusters including interneurons, vulnerable motor neurons, and motor neurons (leptin+).
claims.source: In agreement with our GO analysis of 24hpa ATAC-Seq data, we see an expansion in differentiated neuronal clusters including interneurons, vulnerable motor neurons, and motor neurons (leptin+) at 24hpa.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-Seq analysis.

claims.claim: NSCs are reduced from 38% to 25% at 24hpa.
claims.source: Overall, NSCs are reduced from 38% to 25%, differentiating neurons are reduced from 20% to 10%, and differentiated neurons increase from 42% to 65%.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell type proportions in the single-cell RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Differentiating neurons are reduced from 20% to 10% at 24hpa.
claims.source: Overall, NSCs are reduced from 38% to 25%, differentiating neurons are reduced from 20% to 10%, and differentiated neurons increase from 42% to 65%.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell type proportions in the single-cell RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Differentiated neurons increase from 42% to 65% at 24hpa.
claims.source: Overall, NSCs are reduced from 38% to 25%, differentiating neurons are reduced from 20% to 10%, and differentiated neurons increase from 42% to 65%.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell type proportions in the single-cell RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Motor neurons (leptin+) are virtually absent in the uninjured tail but are abundant at 24hpa.
claims.source: As previously described, we noted that motor neurons (leptin+) are virtually absent in the uninjured tail but are abundant at 24hpa (Aztekin et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-Seq data and citation to published research.

claims.claim: The uninjured tail neural lineage has 30% cells predicted in S phase, 16% cells predicted in G2M phase, and 54% cells predicted in G1 phase.
claims.source: The uninjured tail neural lineage has 30% cells predicted in S phase, 16% cells predicted in G2M phase, and 54% cells predicted in G1 phase (Figure 5H/J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle prediction analysis and reference to Figures 5H/J.

claims.claim: At the 24hpa timepoint, the S phase falls to 17%, G2M falls to 7% and G1 increases to 76%.
claims.source: This distribution shifts markedly at the 24hpa timepoint, where the S phase falls to 17%, G2M falls to 7% and G1 increases to 76% (Figure 4I/K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle prediction analysis and reference to Figures 4I/K.

claims.claim: l1cam, uchl1, nsg1 and ass1 are strongly expressed in one or more differentiated neuronal populations but are lowly expressed or absent in NPCs and non-neural cell types by scRNA-SEQ.
claims.source: All these genes are strongly expressed in one or more differentiated neuronal populations but are lowly expressed or absent in NPCs and non-neural cell types by scRNA-SEQ (Figure 5A–C,G–I,M–O,S–U).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 5A-C, G-I, M-O, S-U showing gene expression.

claims.claim: l1cam, uchl1, nsg1 and ass1 are most strongly and distinctly expressed in the neural ampulla at 24hpa when examined by ISH.
claims.source: When examined by ISH all four genes are most strongly and distinctly expressed in the neural ampulla at 24hpa (Figure 5E,K,Q,W).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 5E, K, Q, W.

claims.claim: Proliferative cells are significantly more abundant at 72hpa relative to 24hpa.
claims.source: As a further test of the hypothesis that proliferation is not prioritized until 72hpa, we used phospho-histone H3 (PH3) staining to quantify mitotic cells in optical longitudinal sections of the spinal cord that overlap with the pax6 domain, finding that proliferative cells are significantly more abundant at 72hpa relative to 24hpa (Figure 5Y-AA).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by PH3 staining quantification shown in Figures 5Y-AA.

claims.claim: Meis1 is predicted as a regulatory factor that binds motifs near runx2 and etv1 at 24hpa.
claims.source: One circuit predicts Meis1 as a regulatory factor that binds motifs near runx2 and etv1 at 24hpa, and Etv1 as a regulatory factor that binds motifs near pbx3 at 24hpa (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene regulatory network prediction analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Etv1 is predicted as a regulatory factor that binds motifs near pbx3 at 24hpa.
claims.source: One circuit predicts Meis1 as a regulatory factor that binds motifs near runx2 and etv1 at 24hpa, and Etv1 as a regulatory factor that binds motifs near pbx3 at 24hpa (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene regulatory network prediction analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: etv1, meis1, pbx3, and runx2 are all expressed in the neural cells.
claims.source: In our scRNA-Seq dataset, etv1, meis1, pbx3, and runx2 are all expressed in the neural cells and are therefore reasonable candidates to regulate neural cell fate transitions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: pbx3 was the most restricted to the neural lineage among etv1, meis1, pbx3, and runx2.
claims.source: Of these, pbx3 was the most restricted to the neural lineage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,G), and was found in several neuronal cell types.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,G showing gene expression.

claims.claim: Pbx3 and Meis1 are homeodomain transcription factors thought to coregulate targets in B-cell leukemia and proximal-distal patterning of the regenerating axolotl limb.
claims.source: Pbx3 and Meis1 are homeodomain transcription factors thought to coregulate targets in B-cell leukemia and proximal-distal patterning of the regenerating axolotl limb (Li et al., 2016; Mercader et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: Meis1 is well-studied for its roles in neural crest and posterior neural fate specification, working together with Pbx1 in Xenopus.
claims.source: In Xenopus, Meis1 is well-studied for its roles in neural crest and posterior neural fate specification, working together with Pbx1 (Kelly et al., 2006; Maeda et al., 2001; Maeda et al., 2002; Salzberg et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: Neither pbx3 nor meis1 have been described in neural regeneration.
claims.source: Neither pbx3 nor meis1 have been described in neural regeneration, and so we decided to probe the function of these genes in neural development and regeneration in Xenopus.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the absence of prior literature on these genes in neural regeneration.

claims.claim: A large fraction (26/61) of Pbx3 targets are shared with Meis1.
claims.source: A large fraction (26/61) of Pbx3 targets are shared with Meis1 (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6B showing Venn diagram of target regions.

claims.claim: Meis1's target peaks are preferentially increased in accessibility at 24hpa.
claims.source: Meis1's target peaks are preferentially increased in accessibility at 24hpa, while Pbx3's are overall increased at 72hpa.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the ATAC-Seq differential accessibility analysis.

claims.claim: Pbx3's target peaks are overall increased at 72hpa.
claims.source: Meis1's target peaks are preferentially increased in accessibility at 24hpa, while Pbx3's are overall increased at 72hpa.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the ATAC-Seq differential accessibility analysis.

claims.claim: Following injury, at 24hpa, expression of meis1 increased to 30% of all neural cells.
claims.source: Following injury, at 24hpa, expression of meis1 increased to 30% of all neural cells (Figure 6F, upper right), driven by increases in interneurons (IN), dopaminergic neuron (DN), and especially motor neuron (MN) clusters (Figure 6E, top).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 6E and 6F showing gene expression.

claims.claim: At 24hpa expression of pbx3 increased to 11% of all neural cells.
claims.source: At 24hpa expression of pbx3 increased to 11% of all neural cells (Figure 6F bottom right), driven by a strong increase in motor neuron expression (Figure 6E, bottom).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 6E and 6F showing gene expression.

claims.claim: At stage 41, both meis1 and pbx3 are expressed in the uninjured brain and spinal cord.
claims.source: At stage 41, both meis1 and pbx3 are expressed in the uninjured brain and spinal cord (Figure 6G–J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 6G-J.

claims.claim: By 24hpa, expression of both meis1 and pbx3 increases in the spinal cord.
claims.source: However, by 24hpa, expression of both factors increases in the spinal cord (Figure 6M,N).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 6M,N.

claims.claim: By 72hpa, expression of meis1 and pbx3 persists more weakly in the spinal cord.
claims.source: By 72hpa, expression persists more weakly in the spinal cord.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization observations.

claims.claim: Knockdown of either Meis1 or Pbx3 resulted in a similar phenotype in stage 41 tadpoles that included small or missing eyes, a shorter anteroposterior body axis and reduced pigment cell population.
claims.source: Knockdown of either Meis1 or Pbx3 resulted in a similar phenotype in stage 41 tadpoles that included small or missing eyes, a shorter anteroposterior body axis and reduced pigment cell population (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: The second set of morpholinos phenocopy the original morpholino injections.
claims.source: We followed up on these phenotypes by repeating the injections with a second set of morpholinos against Pbx3 and Meis1. The second set of morpholinos phenocopy the original morpholino injections (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E,F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E,F.

claims.claim: CRISPR guide RNAs targeting meis1 or pbx3 together with Cas9 protein phenocopy the morpholino effects.
claims.source: As a further confirmation, we designed and injected CRISPR guide RNAs targeting each of these genes together with Cas9 protein at the 4 cell stage, and were able to phenocopy the morpholino effects with this strategy as well (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G–J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G-J.

claims.claim: Stage 41 morphants stained with anti-neurofilament antibody had mispatterned spinal cord and intersomitic axons.
claims.source: When we stained stage 41 morphants with anti-neurofilament antibody, we found that their spinal cord and intersomitic axons were mispatterned, suggesting Meis1 and Pbx3 are necessary for proper development of the nervous system (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B-F.

claims.claim: Neither Meis1 nor Pbx3 vivo-MO caused gross morphological defects when delivered at late tailbud stage.
claims.source: Neither vivo-MO caused gross morphological defects when delivered this way, but both vivo-MOs resulted in reduced axons in the spinal cord as assayed by neurofilament stains at stage 41 (Figure 7C,D), relative to control tadpoles injected with tracer only (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by vivo-morpholino experiments shown in Figures 7B-D.

claims.claim: Both Meis1 and Pbx3 vivo-MOs resulted in reduced axons in the spinal cord as assayed by neurofilament stains at stage 41.
claims.source: Neither vivo-MO caused gross morphological defects when delivered this way, but both vivo-MOs resulted in reduced axons in the spinal cord as assayed by neurofilament stains at stage 41 (Figure 7C,D), relative to control tadpoles injected with tracer only (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by vivo-morpholino experiments shown in Figures 7B-D.

claims.claim: At 72hpa, both Pbx3 and Meis1 knockdown tadpoles have reduced and disorganized neurofilament staining relative to tracer-injected controls.
claims.source: At 72hpa, both Pbx3 and Meis1 knockdown tadpoles have reduced and disorganized neurofilament staining relative to tracer-injected controls (Figure 7F,G, compare with E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 7E-G.

claims.claim: Both Meis1 and Pbx3 knockdown tadpoles have significantly shorter regenerated tails and spinal cords relative to tracer-injected control tadpoles at 72hpa.
claims.source: We quantified the length of the regenerated tail in control and knockdown tadpoles at 72hpa, and found that both Meis1 and Pbx3 knockdown tadpoles have significantly shorter regenerated tails and spinal cords relative to tracer-injected control tadpoles (Figure 7K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 7K.

claims.claim: Spinal cord area is significantly reduced in both Meis1 and Pbx3 morphants at 72hpa.
claims.source: Spinal cord area (measured in confocal optical longitudinal sections) is also significantly reduced in both morphants at 72hpa (Figure 7L)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 7L.

claims.claim: The density of PH3 positive nuclei is not significantly changed relative to controls in Meis1 and Pbx3 morphants.
claims.source: although the density of PH3 positive nuclei is not significantly changed relative to controls (Figure 7H–J,M).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figures 7H-J,M.

claims.claim: Meis1 and Pbx3 are required for proper neural development and for proper regeneration of the tail and spinal cord.
claims.source: We conclude that Meis1 and Pbx3 are not only required for proper neural development but also for proper regeneration of the tail and spinal cord.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the combined results of morpholino and CRISPR experiments.

claims.claim: By isolating neural progenitors, we are able to identify a unique chromatin landscape for these cells, including regulatory peaks that cannot be detected in bulk tissue analysis.
claims.source: By isolating neural progenitors, we are able to identify a unique chromatin landscape for these cells, including regulatory peaks that cannot be detected in bulk tissue analysis.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the ATAC-Seq analysis comparing pax6+ cells to bulk tissue.

claims.claim: pax6+ neural progenitors place a high priority on neuronal differentiation, and specifically on formation of interneurons and motor neuron subtypes by 24hpa.
claims.source: We find that pax6+ neural progenitors place an early priority on neuronal differentiation, and specifically on formation of interneurons and motor neuron subtypes by 24hpa, shown as a model in Figure 8A–C.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the combined ATAC-Seq and scRNA-Seq analysis.

claims.claim: By 24hpa, pax6+ neural progenitors accessibilize genes associated with proliferation and self-renewal at 72hpa.
claims.source: Using both ATAC-Seq and scRNA-Seq, we show that by 24 hr post amputation (hpa), pax6+ neural progenitors place a high priority on differentiation to motor and interneuron subtypes, and only later at 72hpa do they accessibilize genes associated with proliferation and self-renewal.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the ATAC-Seq analysis showing differential accessibility at 72hpa.

claims.claim: pax6+ progenitors prioritize differentiation before proliferation in regeneration, which represents an intriguing counterpoint to embryonic development.
claims.source: Our finding that pax6+ progenitors prioritize differentiation before proliferation in regeneration represents an intriguing counterpoint to embryonic development, in which regional-specific proliferative neural progenitors can only later make the decision to undergo neurogenesis and exit the cell cycle (Hardwick et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison to published research on embryonic development.

claims.claim: There is little proliferation after tail amputation prior to 48hpa.
claims.source: Our model agrees with numerous findings that there is little proliferation after tail amputation prior to 48hpa (Contreras et al., 2009; Gaete et al., 2012; Love et al., 2011; Pelzer et al., 2020; Tsujioka et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: Bulk RNA-Seq analysis shows a transcriptional upregulation of axonogenesis and other neuronal differentiation genes during regeneration.
claims.source: and with bulk RNA-Seq analysis showing a transcriptional upregulation of axonogenesis and other neuronal differentiation genes (Chang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: The identities of specific neural cell types are readily assigned to the same clusters both before and after tail transection in Xenopus.
claims.source: The identities of specific neural cell types are readily assigned to the same clusters both before and after tail transection in Xenopus.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the single-cell RNA-Seq analysis.

claims.claim: In the axolotl limb, scRNA-Seq shows that different connective tissue cell types lose their unique transcriptional identities early in regeneration and converge on a similar signature, as the blastema forms.
claims.source: In the axolotl limb, scRNA-Seq shows that different connective tissue cell types lose their unique transcriptional identities early in regeneration and converge on a similar signature, as the blastema forms (Gerber et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: Diverse cell types retain well-discriminated transcriptional signatures as regeneration proceeds in Xenopus.
claims.source: While the early Xenopus tail regenerate has also been described as a blastema (Gargioli and Slack, 2004; Tsujioka et al., 2015), its parallels to the axolotl blastema have been debated (Mochii et al., 2007), and our study confirms that diverse cell types retain well-discriminated transcriptional signatures as regeneration proceeds.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-Seq analysis.

claims.claim: Pbx3 and Meis1 are expressed in the regenerating spinal cord, with increased expression in motor neuron subtypes during regeneration.
claims.source: We show that these factors are both expressed in the regenerating spinal cord, with increased expression in motor neuron subtypes during regeneration.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization and scRNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Loss of function of either Pbx3 or Meis1 results in disorganized neurofilament outgrowth with a failure of successful axial tissue regeneration.
claims.source: Loss of function of either factor results in disorganized neurofilament outgrowth with a failure of successful axial tissue regeneration.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by morpholino and CRISPR experiments.

claims.claim: Pbx3 and Meis1 are predicted to bind upstream of several dozen differentially accessible neuronal differentiation factors.
claims.source: These factors are predicted to bind upstream of several dozen differentially accessible neuronal differentiation factors and are thus well-placed to drive the prioritization of neuronal differentiation we observe.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis of ATAC-Seq data.

claims.claim: Loss of either Pbx3 or Meis1 does not result in a failure to form neurofilaments, but does result in grossly disrupted organization of neurofilaments and reduced regeneration of the tail and spinal cord.

claims.claim: pbx3 and meis1 are critical regulators of neural development and regeneration.
claims.source: We computationally identify multiple candidate regulators of neural progenitor fate decisions in a regenerative context, and specifically highlight pbx3 and meis1 as critical regulators of neural development and regeneration.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the combined computational analysis and loss-of-function experiments.

results.result: The pax6:GFP transgenic line labels neural progenitor cells (NPCs) in the spinal cord during development and regeneration. GFP expression colocalizes with the NSC marker Sox2 around the central canal, distinct from differentiated neuron markers in the periphery. GFP+ cells are detected in the regenerating tail as early as 6hpa, populate the neural ampulla by 24hpa, and are distributed along the anteroposterior axis by 72hpa.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C12 provide converging evidence from immunofluorescence (Figures 1D-F) and time-course imaging (Figure 1G) that the pax6:GFP line appropriately labels NPCs during regeneration. The spatial and temporal patterns are well-documented with appropriate controls and markers.

results.result: ATAC-Seq analysis of FACS-sorted pax6:GFP+ cells reveals a distinct chromatin accessibility landscape compared to bulk tissue. The pax6 libraries cluster separately from all-tissue libraries by MDS analysis, with 3604 regions more accessible in pax6+ cells showing enrichment for neural-specific GO terms (Neurogenesis, Nervous system development, Neuron differentiation), while 5251 regions more accessible in bulk tissue relate to general cellular processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 and C65 are well-supported by the ATAC-Seq data (Figures 2B-G), including appropriate quality controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), MDS clustering, peak distribution analysis, and GO enrichment. The cell-type-specific approach successfully identifies regulatory regions not detectable in bulk analysis, as demonstrated by the pax6 promoter example.

results.result: Time-resolved ATAC-Seq analysis reveals temporal prioritization of cellular processes during regeneration. At 6hpa, genes associated with nephron tubule morphogenesis and neural patterning are preferentially accessible. At 24hpa, neuron development genes show peak accessibility that is subsequently lost by 72hpa. Cell cycle and proliferation terms are notably absent at 6hpa and 24hpa.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 and C23 are supported by differential accessibility analysis across timepoints (Figures 3D-E, 3H) with appropriate GO term analysis and ReviGO reduction. The temporal dynamics are clearly visualized in heatmaps showing accessibility changes. The absence of proliferation terms at early timepoints is a negative result that supports the overall model.

results.result: At 72hpa, chromatin accessibility shifts to prioritize neural precursor cell proliferation. Five main GO families are enriched at this timepoint, including neuronal precursor cell proliferation. The regions calling this term are more accessible at 72hpa than 24hpa, though approximately half are not differentially accessible compared to uninjured tails.
results.evaluation: Claims C22 and C24 are supported by GO analysis (Figure 3F) and accessibility heatmaps (Figure 3I). The observation that some proliferation-associated regions return to baseline accessibility suggests a return to homeostatic regulation, which is a nuanced and well-documented finding.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-Seq analysis identifies eight distinct neural cell subtypes that maintain their transcriptional identities during regeneration. A total of 781 uninjured and 296 24hpa cells cluster into neural populations including spinal cord progenitors, floor plate progenitors, differentiating neurons, interneurons, motor neurons, vulnerable motor neurons, motor neurons (leptin+), and dopaminergic neurons. Unlike axolotl limb connective tissues, Xenopus neural cells retain well-discriminated transcriptional signatures throughout regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27, C71, and C73 are well-supported by scRNA-Seq analysis (Figures 4A-B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The identification of cell types is based on established markers and differential expression analysis. The comparison to axolotl is appropriately cited and represents an important biological distinction between regeneration models.

results.result: At 24hpa, the composition of neural cell populations shifts toward differentiated neurons. NSCs decrease from 38% to 25%, differentiating neurons decrease from 20% to 10%, and differentiated neurons increase from 42% to 65%. This includes expansion of interneurons, vulnerable motor neurons, and motor neurons (leptin+), with the latter being virtually absent in uninjured tails but abundant at 24hpa.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 are supported by quantitative analysis of cell type proportions in scRNA-Seq data (Figures 4D-G). The sunburst diagrams clearly show the shifts in cell populations. The leptin+ motor neuron observation is consistent with prior published work (Aztekin et al., 2019), providing independent validation.

results.result: Cell cycle analysis reveals a shift from proliferative to quiescent states at 24hpa. In uninjured tails, 30% of neural cells are in S phase, 16% in G2M, and 54% in G1. At 24hpa, S phase drops to 17%, G2M to 7%, and G1 increases to 76%.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by Seurat cell cycle prediction analysis (Figures 4H-K). The dramatic shift toward G1 phase at 24hpa is consistent with the observed increase in differentiated neurons and decrease in proliferating progenitors. However, the analysis relies on computational prediction rather than direct cell cycle measurement, which is a limitation.

results.result: Validation of differentiation markers confirms the temporal model. Four genes (l1cam, uchl1, nsg1, ass1) are strongly expressed in differentiated neurons but not NPCs by scRNA-Seq, and show distinct expression in the neural ampulla at 24hpa by in situ hybridization. Proliferative cells (PH3+) are significantly more abundant at 72hpa compared to 24hpa.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 are supported by orthogonal validation methods: scRNA-Seq (Figures 5A-C, G-I, M-O, S-U), in situ hybridization (Figures 5E, K, Q, W), and immunofluorescence with quantification (Figures 5Y-AA). The convergence of multiple independent methods strengthens confidence in the temporal model of differentiation preceding proliferation.

results.result: Integrative analysis of ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq data predicts gene regulatory networks involving Meis1, Etv1, Pbx3, and Runx2. Meis1 is predicted to bind motifs near runx2 and etv1 at 24hpa, while Etv1 binds near pbx3. All four factors are expressed in neural cells by scRNA-Seq, with pbx3 being most restricted to the neural lineage. Pbx3 and Meis1 are predicted to bind upstream of several dozen differentially accessible neuronal differentiation factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 and C76 are supported by computational integration of ATAC-Seq motif analysis with RNA-Seq expression data (Figure 6A). The predictions are based on established motif databases (HOMER) and are constrained by expression data. However, these remain computational predictions requiring experimental validation, which is appropriately pursued in subsequent experiments.

results.result: Pbx3 and Meis1 are homeodomain transcription factors with established roles in other contexts but not previously studied in neural regeneration. They are known to coregulate targets in B-cell leukemia and axolotl limb regeneration, and Meis1 works with Pbx1 in Xenopus neural development.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 and C80-C82 are appropriately cited to published literature. The novelty claim (C45, C82) regarding neural regeneration is supported by the absence of prior literature, though this is inherently difficult to prove definitively. The background establishes the biological plausibility of these factors as regulators.

results.result: Pbx3 and Meis1 have overlapping but temporally distinct target profiles. A large fraction (26/61) of Pbx3 targets are shared with Meis1. Meis1's target peaks are preferentially increased in accessibility at 24hpa, while Pbx3's targets are overall increased at 72hpa.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by ATAC-Seq differential accessibility analysis and motif analysis (Figures 6B-D). The temporal distinction in target accessibility suggests these factors may have both shared and temporally distinct functions during regeneration.

results.result: Expression of meis1 and pbx3 increases during regeneration. At 24hpa, meis1 expression increases to 30% of neural cells (driven by interneurons, dopaminergic neurons, and motor neurons) and pbx3 to 11% (driven by motor neurons). Both genes are expressed in uninjured brain and spinal cord at stage 41, with expression increasing in the spinal cord by 24hpa and persisting more weakly at 72hpa.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are supported by scRNA-Seq quantification (Figures 6E-F) and in situ hybridization (Figures 6G-P). The convergence of single-cell and spatial expression data provides strong evidence for the temporal and cell-type-specific expression patterns.

results.result: Loss-of-function experiments demonstrate that Meis1 and Pbx3 are required for proper neural development. Morpholino knockdown of either gene results in similar phenotypes including small/missing eyes, shorter body axis, reduced pigmentation, and mispatterned spinal cord and intersomitic axons. These phenotypes are reproduced with a second set of morpholinos and with CRISPR/Cas9.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 are well-supported by multiple independent loss-of-function approaches (Figures 7—figure supplement 1, 7—figure supplement 2). The use of two different morpholinos per gene and CRISPR validation addresses concerns about off-target effects. The developmental phenotypes establish that these factors are necessary for neural development.

results.result: Vivo-morpholino knockdown at late tailbud stage reveals regeneration-specific requirements for Meis1 and Pbx3. Neither vivo-MO causes gross morphological defects, but both result in reduced axons at stage 41 and reduced/disorganized neurofilament staining at 72hpa. Both knockdowns produce significantly shorter regenerated tails and spinal cords with reduced spinal cord area, though PH3+ cell density is not significantly changed.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 are supported by vivo-morpholino experiments with appropriate controls (Figures 7B-M). The late-stage injection strategy cleverly bypasses early developmental defects to assess regeneration-specific functions. The quantification of tail length, spinal cord area, and PH3+ cells provides multiple readouts. The lack of change in PH3+ density suggests the defect is not primarily in proliferation, consistent with the proposed role in differentiation.

results.result: Meis1 and Pbx3 are critical regulators of neural development and regeneration. Loss of function results in disorganized neurofilament outgrowth and failure of successful tail and spinal cord regeneration. The factors are expressed in the regenerating spinal cord with increased expression in motor neuron subtypes, and loss of either factor does not prevent neurofilament formation but disrupts organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C74, C75, C77, and C85 synthesize the expression and functional data. The conclusion that these factors are 'critical regulators' is supported by the convergence of expression patterns, predicted regulatory targets, and loss-of-function phenotypes. The distinction between formation and organization of neurofilaments is an important mechanistic insight.

results.result: Neural progenitors temporally uncouple differentiation and proliferation during regeneration, prioritizing differentiation of motor neuron and interneuron subtypes at 24hpa before accessibilizing proliferation genes at 72hpa. This represents a contrast to embryonic development where proliferation precedes differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68, C83-C84 represent the central model of the paper, supported by converging evidence from ATAC-Seq (temporal GO enrichment), scRNA-Seq (cell type composition and cell cycle analysis), and validation experiments (ISH, PH3 staining). The comparison to embryonic development is appropriately cited (C68). This temporal uncoupling is a novel and well-supported finding.

results.result: Pbx3 and Meis1 may contribute to ongoing differentiation of neuronal structures from 24hpa to 72hpa, and reduced tail regeneration following their loss may be due to interactions between regenerating nerves and other axial structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are speculative interpretations (appropriately indicated by 'may' and 'propose'). While the temporal expression patterns and target accessibility support a role in ongoing differentiation, the mechanism by which neural defects lead to reduced overall tail regeneration is not directly tested. The nerve-dependence hypothesis is plausible and cited, but remains speculative in this context.

results.result: The temporal model agrees with published findings that proliferation is minimal before 48hpa and that axonogenesis and neuronal differentiation genes are transcriptionally upregulated during early regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 appropriately cite multiple published studies that support the temporal model. This agreement with prior bulk RNA-Seq and other analyses provides independent validation of the findings and places them in the context of the existing literature.

results.result: Background claims establish the regenerative capacity of Xenopus tadpoles, the re-expression of developmental genes during regeneration, differences between axolotl and Xenopus regeneration, and the role of Pax6 in neural development.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 are appropriately cited background information from published literature. These establish the biological context and rationale for the study. All claims are supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed research.
